item.title: Village offers insights on serving people
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29
Village offers insights on serving people Eased administrative burden gives Party officials more time for residents' needs For years, village officials in Gangzhongping, in Central China's Hunan province, have spent part of each summer holiday visiting households to raise awareness of drowning risks and help keep children safe. They identify children staying in the village, which has several bodies of water, and they record their ages and school schedules and advise parents or other guardians on water safety. They also check whether children who normally live elsewhere have returned for the holidays and follow up when their whereabouts change. The measures are simple but effective, said Dai Liping, the village's Party branch secretary. Since the work began, Gangzhongping has recorded no drowning incidents of children, and neither have any electrical or traffic accidents involving children been recorded, Dai said. Gangzhongping's bodies of water include a small reservoir. Dai said that frequently seeing news reports of children drowning during the summer holidays had prompted concern about the risks facing children in the village. "The loss of a child would be devastating for a family," Dai said, adding that preventing such tragedies was an important part of serving residents. Under a rotating office-duty arrangement, the village's three officials no longer all spend the entire working day in the office. Those not on duty have more time to visit households, walk through the fields and follow up on residents' needs. These tasks are not difficult in themselves, Dai said, but officials had previously been tied up with too many administrative requirements. As those burdens eased, their focus shifted from paperwork to practical work for residents. In 2019, a national effort to reduce unnecessary administrative burdens gave village officials more time to visit households and respond to residents' needs. Summer water-safety work was among the tasks they took up that year. In March that year, acting on instructions from Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, the General Office of the CPC Central Committee issued a notice calling for action against pointless formalities, easing burdens on grassroots officials and encouraging them to take responsibility and act. On days away from office duty, Dai checks food preparation and cleanliness at the village's mutual-aid center for older residents, inspects sanitation around the village and visits people who need assistance. Dai also follows the village's agricultural projects, checking the growth of golden chrysanthemums and contacting potential buyers ahead of a planned harvest this month. In March 2024, Xi visited Gangzhongping village during a fact-finding trip to Hunan. He examined efforts to reduce burdens on grassroots officials and called for persistent action against pointless formalities and bureaucratism and for streamlining administration. Joseph Olivier Mendo'o, a Cameroonian who has visited more than 60 villages in over 20 Chinese provinces, visited Gangzhongping in July and November 2025. He said cutting redundant paperwork so that officials could spend more time visiting households reflects a shift he has observed across rural China. "In Gangzhongping, I saw this reclaimed time turn into tangible care: checking on children's safety, listening quietly to farming families' worries, and sorting out small, urgent problems before they escalate," Mendo'o said. He saw a similar pattern in villages in Zhejiang and Guizhou provinces. "Party members do not wait for complaints to arrive at a desk; they walk the lanes, keep track of vulnerable households, and tailor solutions to what villagers actually need," he said. "This is where discipline and conduct translate into service: Strengthening Party discipline is not an abstract rule from above," he said. "It is a practical mechanism that keeps grassroots cadres accountable, refocuses their energy away from formalities, and anchors governance in face-to-face contact with residents." During deliberations with the Jiangsu delegation to the fourth session of the 14th National People's Congress in March this year, Xi stressed that more effective Party governance provides a stronger guarantee for economic and social development. He also called for earning public trust through tangible results in full and rigorous Party self-governance and pooling strength to advance development. The fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, being held in Beijing from Monday to Thursday, is considering a draft decision on sustained efforts to advance full and rigorous Party self-governance. The CPC had more than 101 million members and about 5.43 million primary-level Party organizations at the end of 2025, according to a statistical bulletin released by the Organization Department of the CPC Central Committee. Gu Shaojie, an associate professor at the China Executive Leadership Academy Yan'an, said that improving governance capacity is an integral requirement of full and rigorous Party self-governance. "Full and rigorous Party self-governance is not about being strict for its own sake," Gu said. One of its fundamental purposes, he added, is to improve the Party's ability to lead the modernization drive and translate its political and organizational strengths into effective governance. At a group study session of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee on June 27, 2024, Xi called for strengthening grassroots Party organizations' ability to lead local governance as part of efforts to improve the systems for full and rigorous Party self-governance. In Gangzhongping, Dai, the village's Party branch secretary, said household visits also help officials understand residents' employment circumstances and match them with local job opportunities. When a village workshop that offers traditional food-making experiences and is linked to an employment service station needed a full-time manager, officials identified Liu Qin through information gathered about local households, Dai said. The 40-year-old mother of three had relied on casual work and small trading activities. Her husband worked away from home, while her elderly mother-in-law could only offer limited help with the children. Liu now earns 3,000 yuan ($450) a month. Her work includes liaising with villagers who supply agricultural products to the workshop, where visitors can try traditional activities such as tofu-making and preparing the local specialty leicha, or pounded tea. The income allows her to support herself and contribute to a pension program for people in flexible employment, Liu said. Gu, the professor, said that once policies are determined, officials' ability to carry them out becomes decisive. He cited the decision adopted at the fourth plenary session of the 19th CPC Central Committee in 2019, which identified improving governance capacity as a major task in building the ranks of officials in the new era. Governance capacity does not merely benefit from full and rigorous Party self-governance; it also helps drive that process forward, Gu said. Stronger governance capabilities enable Party organizations to identify and address underlying problems in Party self-governance through more law-based, standardized and precise methods, he said. The purpose of strengthening Party discipline, said Mendo'o, the Cameroonian who has visited many villages in China, "is to make public services more human, precise and people-centered". Contact the writers at mojingxi@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: At least 68 killed in Spain train collision
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29
At least 68 killed in high-speed train collision in Spain Rescue crews and crash investigators were combing through the wreckage on Wednesday after two high-speed trains collided near Toledo in central Spain. At least 68 people were killed in the accident, authorities said. The crash involved a passenger train operated by Spain's state-owned national railway company Renfe, and one operated by the country's first private high-speed rail company, Iryo. The collision shortly after 9 am local time caused several carriages from the Iryo train to fully derail, according to a government spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha autonomous region, where the accident happened. The official added that the cause and the final death toll were not immediately known. The number of confirmed deaths from the train crash has reached 68, Castilla-La Mancha's regional government said on Wednesday. A spokesperson for ADIF, the state-owned company that manages Spain's railway infrastructure, said the incident happened between the towns of Mora and Orgaz, and that the trains were both traveling from Madrid to Seville when one slammed into the other train while it was stationary. ADIF added in a message on X: "Traffic on the Madrid-Andalusia high-speed rail line has been suspended following a rear-end collision between two trains." Iryo said it had also triggered "all emergency protocols" to ascertain what happened. "This morning, our train 6076, traveling from Madrid to Seville, was involved in an accident near Urda, at kilometer point 118," the company said, adding it was "working closely with the relevant authorities to manage the situation". It added that all services from Madrid's Atocha station bound for Spain's south had been canceled, and that "at this time, there is no estimate for when service will be restored". The Independent newspaper quoted Manuel Galan, the mayor of Urda, the small municipality where the accident happened, as saying the emergency services had asked him to make a sports hall available to accommodate injured passengers and to mount a triage operation. The Spanish newspaper El Pais quoted federal coordinator Antonio Maillo as saying he feared for "the worst" after the "very serious accident" and that the death toll was likely to rise. The Renfe train had 397 passengers on board at the time, while the Iryo train had 147. The Chinese embassy in Spain has confirmed that four Chinese nationals were aboard the trains involved in the collision, with at least one sustaining minor injuries. Political parties across Spain canceled scheduled activities on Wednesday, while officials expressed their condolences for those affected. Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said he was "shocked by the serious train accident" and was in constant contact with his transport minister and other relevant authorities. A spokesperson for Spain's emergency services told Agence France-Presse shortly after the collision that "all resources" were being deployed, including "several fire crews, three helicopters, and two mobile intensive care units". Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia said in a short statement on X that they were following news of the accident. "We are deeply saddened and concerned by the train accident in Urda (Toledo)," the royal couple said. "We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected." The crash was the latest in a series of tragic accidents that have plagued Spain's railway system. In January, a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain into the path of an oncoming Renfe train, resulting in 46 deaths. Xinhua and agencies contributed to this story.

item.title: Tianjin's Xibeijiao serves up a taste of local life
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29
In Tianjin's Xibeijiao neighborhood, getting breakfast can be an early-morning test of patience. Xibeijiao's eateries attract crowds well before much of the city is fully awake, and by midmorning, finding a place to sit down can be a challenge. For those who make it early, the reward is a hearty breakfast and a glimpse of the city starting its day. Steam rises from baskets of buns, pancakes sizzle on hot griddles and freshly fried snacks emerge from busy kitchens. Customers line up at familiar stalls, pick up breakfast to go or pause to eat before heading off to work. The experience offers a different way to discover Tianjin, a port city in northern China better known to many visitors for its European-style architecture, historical streets and riverfront. Lin Yaqi, a visitor from Singapore, made a special trip to the neighborhood with her friends in mid-October after seeing enthusiastic recommendations online. They tasted jianbing guozi, steamed buns and snacks they had never tried before. "There were so many choices," Lin recalled. "You walk just a few steps and there's another shop, and everything smelled so good!" She was particularly taken with jianbing guozi, a Tianjin breakfast staple made by spreading mung bean batter on a hot griddle, cracking an egg onto the pancake and folding it around a fried dough stick or a crispy cracker, with sauces added for extra flavor. The appeal lies partly in the combination of textures — the thin, tender pancake, the crispness of the filling and the savory sauces. Prepared fresh to order, it is easy to eat on the way to work, yet substantial enough to keep hunger at bay through the morning. For Lin, having breakfast like a local offered a glimpse of Tianjin beyond its tourist attractions and a way to understand the city through the daily routines of its residents. The mix of food and daily life is what defines Xibeijiao, a historical breakfast hub in Lingdangge subdistrict in Tianjin's Hongqiao district, where food businesses sit alongside homes and neighborhood services. Liu Tao, a senior official of Lingdangge subdistrict, noted that Xibeijiao brings together residential life, commerce and tourism. Many food businesses have been passed down through generations, while the neighborhood's character also reflects the history and food traditions of its Hui ethnic community, he said. Tianjin's history as a trading and transportation hub helps to explain the place of hearty, convenient meals in its food culture. Goods moved through the city along the Grand Canal and its waterways, while workers engaged in loading and transporting goods needed food to sustain long working days. In Xibeijiao, generations of local families helped turn the preparation and sale of traditional snacks into an enduring part of community life. Xu Peng's grandmother began selling jianbing guozi in Tianjin's old Nanshi area in 1958. Xu grew up watching her make the pancakes, and the family opened its shop in Xibeijiao in 2024. For Xu, the appeal of the traditional Tianjin pancake lies in its simplicity. The fillings are basic, and that allows all the flavors to come through. "Too many additions can overwhelm the original taste," he said. The shop serves regular customers as well as visitors curious about how the breakfast staple is made. Its open kitchen lets customers try preparing their own jianbing guozi, turning a quick meal into a hands-on experience. The family has also created themed plush toys as souvenirs, giving visitors a playful reminder of a dish that local residents eat without a second thought. For Xu, introducing visitors to jianbing guozi is also a way of introducing them to the city that gave the dish its character. "We have a responsibility to let visitors to Tianjin experience not only the food, but also the city's local culture, customs and everyday life," he said.

item.title: Australia returns ancient relics to China
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29
Australia handed over to China two Northern Song Dynasty (960-1127) head statues in a major ceremony on Wednesday, the latest repatriation of Chinese relics under joint efforts to protect cultural heritage and build on ties between the two nations. At the National Gallery of Australia in Canberra, senior officials and representatives from both sides witnessed the handover of the head statues of a civil official and a military official, from the Song imperial mausoleums in Gongyi, Central China's Henan province, near the then-capital of Kaifeng. Speaking at the ceremony, Chinese Ambassador to Australia Liu Jinsong said the two statues "once stood quietly guarding the ancient tombs. They have seen the passage of time and traveled across the oceans". According to the National Gallery of Australia, the relics became part of its collection in 1995. China's National Cultural Heritage Administration said in a statement that the restitution process of the statues was initiated with a request to the National Gallery of Australia in 2025 to return them, following investigations and studies by relevant Chinese authorities. The two sides subsequently worked together under international conventions and agreements on the protection of cultural property, and successfully secured the return of the relics to China. The ambassador expressed his heartfelt appreciation to "all the Australian institutions and individuals who have contributed to this return", and thanked the museum and heritage professionals from both countries for their work. "The return of these two statues is not the end of their story. It is a new beginning for research, conservation and cultural heritage," he said. Nick Mitzevich, director of the National Gallery of Australia, said it is committed to the "ethical management of the national collection through due diligence and proactive provenance research". "We value and respect international collaboration and we consider repatriation to be more than a physical return of an object. It is an act of respect, an act of responsibility and an act of world partnership," he said. Tang Wei, deputy director of China's National Cultural Heritage Administration, said that promoting the return of cultural objects lost overseas to their countries of origin is "an act of justice", safeguarding cultural heritage and the "national sentiments of people". He said that government agencies, museums and cultural heritage institutions in China and Australia have worked closely in recent years to honor their commitment to the protection of cultural heritage under international frameworks. The repatriation of the Song statues comes three years after Australia returned five relics to China, including two figurines dating back about 1,400 years ago, and a reptile fossil from northeastern China dating back to between 133 and 120 million years ago. Duan Yong, director of the Center for Research on Chinese Cultural Relics Abroad at Shanghai University, said that over the past decade, the recovery and return of lost cultural relics have shown "a trend that is relatively favorable to countries, including China, that suffered the loss of their cultural heritage". He explained that countries dispossessed of their cultural heritage have continued to make recovery efforts to protect their cultural rights and interests. The spirit of relevant international conventions — such as UNESCO's 1970 Convention and the UNIDROIT 1995 Convention — is gaining wider acceptance, providing an important legal basis for recovery and return. "In the recovery of lost cultural relics, research on provenance and transfer history is very important and plays a decisive role, especially in litigation," he said. "The return of cultural relics by the Australian side was precisely due to sufficient provenance." He called for strengthening research on the provenance and transfer history of lost cultural relics, enhancing registration and filing for relics in domestic collections and private hands, and conducting thorough exploration and investigation of buried relics. Contact the writers at xinxin@chinadaily.com.cn XIN XIN and ALEXIS HOOI in Canberra and DENG ZHANGYU in Beijing

item.title: 'Super students' ride tide of AI innovation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29
'Super students' ride tide of AI innovation School-age creators developing tools, programs to solve real-world problems At just 14, Zhang Shaoqing's prowess with AI tools means he could easily be included in the ranks of the new wave of "super students" but it's a description he balks at. "Daring to imagine and daring to try is encouraging, but it's also a kind of pressure; it's as if I'm not a good student unless I've built something," said the ninth-grader at Wuxi Dipont School of Arts and Science in Jiangsu province. "I don't want to be defined as a 'super student.' I would rather be seen as an ordinary student who has stayed passionate about one field for a long time," he added. His mother Liu Liwei, who has encouraged his development and interests, is also uncomfortable with the super student label, which has recently gained online traction. Many youngsters involved in sophisticated technology projects are not necessarily way ahead of others, but have benefited from opportunities, guidance and supportive environments, she said. "I always remind him not to think he is better than others. He has simply received opportunities that many students may not have had," said Liu. From developing artificial intelligence tools for schools to creating digital content, a growing number of Chinese teenagers are moving from technology users to creators, offering a glimpse into how they are exploring opportunities and challenges in the AI era. In recent years, Chinese school students have begun participating in AI competitions, open-source communities and industry-linked innovation programs once mainly associated with university students and professionals. Tencent Youth Tech Training Camp, launched in 2016, has attracted more than 900,000 users to its platform, partnered with over 2,000 schools and accumulated more than 40,000 works as of September 2026. Dong Xinye, deputy director of the Youth Innovation Education Center at Shenzhen InnoX Academy, an education program that aims to nurture innovative talent for the AI era through project-based learning, said teenagers' participation in AI and innovation programs has grown significantly in recent years. "What was once a niche interest among a small number of technology enthusiasts has gradually become a mainstream way for young people to explore the world," said Dong.

item.title: Alibaba order highlights firms' challenges in US
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28
Alibaba order highlights firms' challenges in US China's Alibaba Group has won a preliminary injunction from a United States court that ordered the US government not to deny Pentagon contracts to companies solely because they, their parent companies or subsidiaries do business with firms that lobby for the e-commerce giant, in yet another example of a Chinese company legally challenging unilateral and discriminatory US business restrictions. US District Judge Eumi K. Lee from California granted Alibaba the preliminary injunction on Monday. The Pentagon had argued that the ban would protect sensitive military information and prevent improper influence. The court said the Pentagon's evidence was insufficient to justify restricting political speech. In a lawsuit filed in June, Alibaba sought its removal from a US Defense Department list of entities allegedly linked to China's military. The group said that it has no military ties and is not part of any military-civil fusion strategy. The Monday injunction suspended the restriction arising from Alibaba's designation but hadn't decided whether the company should be on the list. Tu Xinquan, dean of the China Institute for WTO Studies at the University of International Business and Economics in Beijing, said that national security has become a "catch-all" justification for US business restrictions. He added that the ultimate goal for such lists is to undermine competitive Chinese products and protect US domestic industries. A number of Chinese companies have already secured favorable US court rulings. Chinese pharmaceutical research and manufacturing services group WuXi AppTec secured a preliminary injunction in August, blocking the US Defense Department from enforcing its designation as a Chinese military company under Section 1260H while litigation continued. Chinese lidar manufacturer Hesai Technology also won an important appeal in August. The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit required the government to provide procedural protections. In 2021, Chinese tech company Xiaomi Corp secured a final court order, vacating its designation on the Pentagon's earlier Chinese military companies list. Mei Xinyu, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation in Beijing, said: "In such cases, Chinese (companies) were seeking to guard their equal rights, not legal privileges, on the global stage."

item.title: Former vice-premier Liu Yandong dies at 81
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28
Former vice-premier Liu Yandong dies at 81 Former Chinese vice-premier and state councilor Liu Yandong passed away due to illness at the age of 81 in Beijing on Wednesday. Liu had served as a member of the Political Bureau of the 17th and 18th Central Committees of the Communist Party of China, and vice-chairwoman of the 10th National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, the country's top political advisory body. An official statement described Liu as "an excellent Party member, a time-tested and loyal communist fighter, and an outstanding leader in the CPC's united front work and in China's education, science and technology, healthcare, and work related to women and children". Born in November 1945 in Nantong, Jiangsu province, Liu joined the CPC in July 1964. She studied engineering chemistry at Tsinghua University and later earned a doctorate in law from Jilin University. Liu became a state councilor in 2008 and served as vice-premier of the State Council from 2013 to 2018. She also served as vice-chairwoman of the Beijing Organizing Committee for the 2008 Olympic Games.

item.title: China voices concerns over EU trade curbs
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28
China voices concerns over EU trade curbs China has expressed concern over the European Union's recent push to introduce trade restrictions, noting that such measures have adversely affected industrial and supply chain stability and bilateral business cooperation, the Ministry of Commerce said in a statement on Wednesday. During his meeting with Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament's Committee on International Trade, in Beijing on Tuesday, Commerce Minister Wang Wentao said China and the EU are important economic and trade partners and key supporters of the multilateral trading system. According to the European Parliament, Lange is leading a delegation from its Committee on International Trade to Beijing, Hangzhou in Zhejiang province and Shanghai from Tuesday to Thursday. Wang said two rounds of talks under the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism this year had yielded substantial results, demonstrating both sides' ability to address differences through dialogue. He also warned that the EU's growing use of trade restrictions is disrupting bilateral economic cooperation and putting pressure on cross-border supply chains. "China is not the source of the EU's problems, but a partner in finding solutions," Wang added. The Chinese commerce minister called on the EU to work with China to expand two-way investment, increase China's imports from the bloc and explore cooperation in emerging sectors to promote more balanced bilateral trade in accordance with World Trade Organization rules and the principle of reciprocity and mutual benefit. Lange said that maintaining stable EU-China economic ties is particularly important amid global economic uncertainty. Lange welcomed Chinese investment in Europe and voiced support for WTO reform. He said the committee he chairs supports continued bilateral consultations to manage differences and is willing to play an active role in facilitating dialogue. Under the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism, the first meeting in Brussels in late June established four workstreams and a joint monitoring mechanism to manage trade frictions. The second, held in Beijing in early October, produced 16 points of consensus covering trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights and WTO reform. Sun Chenghao, associate research fellow at Tsinghua University's Center for International Security and Strategy, said continued dialogue offers China and the EU a way to address trade disputes without allowing disagreements in individual sectors to overshadow their broader economic relationship. Beyond trade disputes, economic cooperation continues to offer opportunities for European businesses in China, he said.

item.title: Russian scholar advocates for a 'concert of civilizations'
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28
Russian scholar advocates for a 'concert of civilizations' Alexander A. Dynkin, president of the Primakov National Research Institute of World Economy and International Relations, said at the Global Strategic Dialogue 2026 in Beijing on Wednesday that the multilayer interaction between Russia and China, two nations with distinct civilizational identities, has become a prototype for a new form of global cooperation. Dynkin said the joint production of the visionary idea of the future "concert of civilizations" rather than Huntington's "Clash of Civilizations" is worthy of the efforts of China and Russia. Highlighting the existential challenges facing the world today, Dynkin stressed the urgent need to avoid crossing a point of no return that could lead to major conflict. He called for the development of a new world order framework that prioritizes peace and stability, emphasizing the role of the Global Governance Initiative in achieving this goal.
